checks.claim: Order from lowest to highest frequency: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays; key Microwaves comes next after radio
Wrong choices Infrared, Ultraviolet, X-rays all lie further along than microwaves
Context: waves grow shorter at every step; infrared just past the red; UV and X-rays beyond the violet
Violet about 400 nm; red the longest visible waves, about 700 nm
Key: 650 nm light is red (red 625-750 nm; Grokipedia: red above 620 nm)
Wrong choices: blue 450-485, green 500-565, yellow 565-590 nm, none near 650
Red has the lowest frequency of the colours (about 430 THz), violet the highest (about 790 THz)
Herschel, 1800, glass prism, thermometers with blackened bulbs
Readings climbed from violet to red; just beyond the red, where no light showed, the highest temperature of all
Key: invisible rays in sunlight
Wrong choices: room warming, prism warmed, black paint warming in the dark, ruled out by the two blackened control thermometers placed beyond the spectrum
checks.note: IPAC: 'the other two were placed beyond the spectrum as control samples'; Linda Hall: controls 'registering room temperature' (https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/william-herschel-4/).

checks.claim: Context: the rays reflect and bend as light does; called calorific rays; now called infrared
Context: 'Herschel found that the invisible rays reflect and bend through glass just as light does, so they were a kind of light from the Sun'
checks.note: True in modern terms (IPAC: 'a form of light (or radiation) beyond red light'), but the 'so' reads as Herschel's own conclusion. His later 1800 paper set out to decide whether the rays of heat and light were 'the same, or different', stressed that the heat and light maxima did not coincide, and he came to treat them as distinct (APS News, Feb 2024, gives the same reading). Fix: '...just as light does. They are now known to be a kind of light: he called them calorific rays, and they are now called infrared.'

checks.claim: Ritter, 1801, motivated by Herschel's heat rays; prism, darkened room, silver chloride paper strips along the spectrum and beyond
Key: darkened fastest just beyond the violet end
checks.note: Wikipedia: rays just past violet 'darkened silver chloride-soaked paper more quickly than violet light itself'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: beyond red, yellow, violet itself; darkening was weakest toward red and strongest past violet
Silver chloride is a salt that darkens in light
Context: Ritter called them chemical rays; ultraviolet means beyond the violet
Röntgen, Würzburg, 1895; discharge (Hittorf/Crookes) tube wrapped in black cardboard; darkened room
A coated (barium platinocyanide) screen glowed across the room, even behind a book of a thousand pages
checks.note: His paper: fluorescence 'still visible at two metres distance'; screen lights 'behind a book of a thousand pages'. 'Across his darkened room' is loose for about two metres but not wrong; 'a metre or two away' would be exact.

checks.claim: Anna Bertha's hand on a photographic plate (22 Dec 1895): bones and wedding ring visible, flesh faint
Key: bone stops more rays than flesh; wrong choices (lets more through, emits rays, reflects them) are wrong
checks.note: Paper: 'the shadow shows the bones clearly'; density 'mainly affects their permeability'.

checks.claim: Context: glass hardly absorbs microwaves; metal walls reflect
Key: thermal camera picks up infrared given off by a warm body
Wrong choices: reflected IR from a lamp (active IR, not thermal), brightened visible light (image intensifier), UV from skin
checks.note: Thermography 'differs fundamentally from night-vision technologies that employ image intensification'; NASA: humans 'only emit infrared waves'.

checks.claim: Context: works in total darkness and through smoke; TV remotes use infrared
Context: a body at 37 C 'gives off far more' infrared than the cool ground and trees
checks.note: Radiated power goes as the fourth power of absolute temperature, so warm skin (about 305 K) against ground at about 280 K gives off only about 1.4 to 1.7 times as much; the camera shows him brightly because it maps small differences. 'Far more' overstates it. Fix: 'gives off more than the cooler ground and trees around it'.

checks.claim: Key: 'Its waves have a higher frequency and carry more energy'
checks.note: Higher frequency means more energy PER PHOTON (E = hf). The stem pits UV against a BRIGHT red lamp, whose light may well carry more energy in total; that a light's waves carry more energy is set by brightness, not frequency, so the key as worded states the classic misconception. Fix the key: 'Each packet of it carries more energy, from its higher frequency' (the context already explains the packets).

checks.claim: UV-C at 254 nm used in drinking water; damages DNA/RNA so germs cannot multiply
Wrong choice: UV waves are longer (UV 100-400 nm, shorter than red)
Wrong choice: UV travels faster through water (water's index is higher in UV, so UV is slower)
checks.note: Index 1.349 at 300 nm vs 1.33 visible.

checks.note: Wikipedia: radiosurgery 'aims to destroy target tissue', though success is often judged as the tumour no longer growing; acceptable simplification.

unit_notes: Band order, speed of light, Herschel, Ritter, Röntgen, Hertz, phone, microwave oven (no resonance myth), Gamma Knife all check out. One error: the UV question's key says UV's waves 'carry more energy' against a BRIGHT red lamp; it must say each packet (photon) carries more. Two uncertain wording points: Herschel context's 'so they were a kind of light' reads as Herschel's own conclusion (he came to think heat and light rays distinct); thermal-camera context's 'far more' infrared overstates a 1.4-1.7x difference.
